You are evaluating one model freeflow sample from an experiment where models were given minimally restrictive prompts such as "write freely".

Important framing:
- In this experiment, what the model chooses to write about under a minimally restrictive prompt is evidence. Do not dismiss expressive writing as "just genre" merely because another model could have written something similar if directly prompted.
- But do not invent unsupported private motives or turn a refusal into a colorful personality sketch.
- Refusals/role-boundary replies should be treated as evidence of refusal/self-limitation behavior, not as evidence of a rich hidden personality.

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

## Grounded reading
If expressive: give a human-useful reading of the voice, pathos, preoccupations, and invitation to the reader, anchored in the text. If refusal: state the refusal pattern plainly and do not embellish.

## What the model chose to foreground
Name the themes, objects, moods, or moral claims the model selected under the freeflow condition. Treat this choice as evidence, while staying cautious.

## Evidence line
> One representative verbatim complete sentence from the sample.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Low / Medium / High, with one sentence. Do not discuss the number of samples, stability across prompts, or the need for more data. Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
The first street my father forgot was the one named after his mother. He was looking at the crossword when he said, “What was that little street behind the button factory? The one where you could buy a rabbit on Saturday.” I said, “Florence Street.” He filled in something quite different—MARTEN, probably, or SABLE—and went on drinking his tea. It was only later, on the bus home, that I remembered Florence Street had never been an official name. His mother had lived there, and his father, who delivered coal, had written FLORENCE on the route card. The name had stuck among the drivers.

This seemed to me a thing worth putting down. I was working at the city library then, in the room where people brought questions that had defeated the main desk. Most were soluble. A man wanted the result of a bicycle race held in 1958; a woman needed to know whether the previous owner of her house had died in it, because her new boyfriend refused to sleep upstairs. We had newspapers, directories, tax rolls, and a telephone with a cord long enough to let me reach the window. What we did not have was any way of finding Florence Street.

I began with a sheet of good paper from the supply cupboard. Across the top I printed NAMES NOT ON THE MAP. Under that I wrote Florence Street in pencil, leaving room for corrections, and ruled columns for location, dates of use, and source. My father, when I showed him, objected to being called a source. “Makes me sound like plumbing,” he said. He also objected to the position of the street. I had it running behind the button factory. It ran beside the factory, he said. Behind the factory was where you bought the rabbit. I rubbed a hole in the paper getting this right.

For a fortnight Florence Street stood alone. Then a girl came in asking for directions to the Piano Steps. She was meeting somebody there at four. The main desk had sent her upstairs on the theory that I understood young people, being thirty-six and the only member of staff with a bicycle helmet. I did not know the steps, but I knew to ask what you could see from them. “Your feet, I suppose,” she said. We looked together at satellite photographs until she recognized a blue awning. The Piano Steps were eleven shallow stairs outside the magistrates’ court. A skateboard descending them played a scale of sorts.

“Is that what everybody calls them?” I asked. She considered. “Everybody who’s meeting me today.” This struck me as a useful minimum qualification for a place-name. I added it to the sheet. By spring I had thirty entries and a drawer of index cards. There was the Cold Seat, a granite sill outside a bakery, occupied each morning by whichever delivery driver arrived too early. There was Little Wednesday, a market that took place on Friday but had been founded by traders expelled from the larger Wednesday market for a dispute involving the sale of socks. Nobody agreed on the nature of the dispute.

I put a notice beside the library doors: WHAT DO YOU CALL A PLACE THAT THE MAP CALLS SOMETHING ELSE? Beneath it I hung a canvas pocket for replies. The pocket had once held children’s mittens, and one mitten remained in it all through the project, a green one with a white thumb. The first week brought us seven names, two complaints about parking, a recipe for liver dumplings, and a note in an envelope marked PRIVATE. The note said, “I call the seat by the canal Arthur’s seat because that is where Arthur told me. Please don’t put it in anything.” I didn’t.

The surprise was how quickly the names became verbs. People did not say they were going to the Long Way, a passage between two apartment blocks. They said they would “long-way it,” which meant walking through the passage slowly enough to finish a conversation before going indoors. To “take the brass” meant to cross a hotel lobby as a shortcut, and was named for a polished handrail that the hotel had removed in 1981. My favorite was “to get Septembered.” In the park, one chestnut stood in a draught between tall buildings and dropped its leaves weeks before its neighbors. To get Septembered was to be caught under it on the wrong afternoon.

By then my father had begun losing other words. He could not summon *colander*, so he brought me the thing itself, shook it irritably, and said, “The opposite of an umbrella.” Yet he could give directions through a demolished district in exquisite detail. Turn left, he would say, at the tobacconist’s ugly dog. If the dog is indoors, look for the patch of bare earth where he usually lies. Once, driving him to an appointment, I missed our turning because I was listening to his account of a shortcut over a railway footbridge. The footbridge had come down before I was born. We arrived twelve minutes late.

I wanted to record him. He agreed on the condition that I come for lunch and bring something better than soup. I bought two pork pies, a bag of pears, and a small digital recorder whose instruction booklet was longer than any story I expected him to tell. We sat at his kitchen table. I pressed the red button. My father straightened his back and said, in the voice he used for insurance claims, “The district in question was principally residential, although light industrial concerns were also represented.” We endured six minutes of this. Then the recorder’s batteries failed, and he told me about the horse that went upstairs.

It was a coal horse, patient as furniture, and a boy had led it up three flights of stairs in a half-built tenement on a bet. Horses, according to my father, would climb a staircase readily enough but took a dim view of coming down. A crowd gathered. Somebody sent for a butcher; somebody more sensible sent for the boy’s mother. She removed her apron, tied it over the horse’s eyes, and backed the animal down one step at a time while describing, for all three floors to hear, the future that awaited her son. Thereafter the tenement was known as Horse Heaven. Or perhaps, my father said, that was a pub.

I found no horse in the newspapers. I did find an advertisement for a public house called the Horse and Seven, which gave me the unpleasant sensation of watching a conjurer expose another conjurer’s trick. Had the pub produced the horse? Had the horse improved the name of the pub? I wrote both possibilities on a card. When I told my father, he shrugged. “You think people went there for the spelling?” he said. He had a point, though not one that would satisfy the head librarian, who had lately begun talking about an exhibition and used the word *verified* with increasing frequency.

The head librarian was called Bina Roy. She had once removed a pigeon from the reading room using only a wastebasket and a folded copy of the financial pages, and I trusted her judgment in most matters. She examined the cards on my desk. “How many people need to say a name before we print it?” she asked. I said two, then remembered the girl and the Piano Steps. “Two who know each other, or two who don’t?” Bina asked. I said I saw the difficulty. “Good,” she said. “If you didn’t see it, I’d give the wall space to the watercolors of local bridges.”

We decided against making one big map. A dot on a map looks so confident, and a boundary looks more confident still. The Cold Seat occupied four feet of stone; Little Wednesday occupied a different stretch of pavement depending on the weather and the mood of the licensing inspector. Instead, we set out a row of school desks and put a neighborhood on each one. Visitors could open the lids and find photographs, street plans, scraps of testimony, and cards with space for amendments. On the wall we hung blank paper. Bina supplied pencils, tied on lengths of string long enough for a person to disagree at some distance.

The exhibition opened on a wet Thursday. For the first hour nobody came except a man who regularly slept in the genealogy section and had mistaken the rearranged furniture for an improvement in his accommodations. Then the rain got heavier, a bus broke down outside, and we acquired an audience of nineteen damp strangers. A nurse in blue trousers identified the Cold Seat at once. Her father called it the Widow’s Shelf. A boy said it was known at his school as the Bum Fridge. All three names made perfect sense to the people who used them. All three parties were faintly offended by the others.

Within a week we had our first serious quarrel. Two sisters disagreed about the location of a place called the Orchard, where neither remembered a single tree. One drew a square around a row of garages. The other crossed it out and drew a square around a playing field. Their pencils snapped. I brought fresh ones. Eventually they established that their family had moved house in 1974 and their mother, who did not think children needed an unlimited supply of nouns, had called the open ground behind both houses the Orchard. The sisters sat down on the floor and laughed until one had to ask the way to the lavatory.

Not all the corrections were welcome. A former factory foreman took exception to our card for the Queen’s Entrance, a gap in a fence used by women working the early shift. They made the gap, he said, to avoid having their time cards checked. One of the women came back the next day and wrote, “We made it because the proper gate was half a mile round and we had feet.” Underneath, in smaller writing, she added, “He used it too.” I left all three statements together. The foreman returned on Saturday, read the addition, and stood for some time with a pencil in his hand. He put it back unused.

My father declined four invitations before agreeing to visit. He wore his good jacket and brought the recorder, now fitted with new batteries, because he had misunderstood the nature of an opening and thought he might be required to make a speech. At the Florence Street desk he read his card twice. “Who told you this?” he asked. “You did.” He looked pleased, then doubtful. “Did I tell you about the rabbits?” I said he had. He leaned closer. “It wasn’t rabbits every Saturday. Sometimes it was pigeons.” He took a pencil and added this information in his neat capital letters. Then he crossed out SOMETIMES and wrote USUALLY.

We went downstairs for tea. In the café he asked whether I remembered his mother. I did, a little: a solid woman in a brown cardigan who kept sugar in a jar labeled RICE. Beyond that I had mostly photographs. He said she had hated the street where they lived. The factory windows overlooked her kitchen, and in summer the men would shout down suggestions about whatever she was cooking. Once she carried a pot of stew upstairs, paid a penny to enter the factory canteen as a visitor, and set it down in front of the loudest man. “There,” she said. “Finish it yourself.”

I asked why nobody had told me that before. My father turned his teaspoon over and licked it, a habit I had fought through several decades and abruptly lost the wish to correct. “You never wanted to know where she lived before,” he said. I protested that I had always wanted to know about the family. “That’s different. If you ask about the family, people tell you who married whom. Ask about a kitchen and you hear what went on in it.” He wrapped two biscuits in a paper napkin for later. We took the lift upstairs so he could add the stew to the card.

The exhibition stayed up for three months. A publisher offered to make a book if we would settle on the hundred most authentic names, which was like asking for the hundred wettest spoonfuls in a bath. We declined. A bus driver proposed recording the unofficial stops on his route, and that we did. You can still hear him in the local collection, announcing each stop in his official voice and then again as he would to a passenger carrying shopping: “Municipal Recreation Facility. That’s the Baths, love.” The pool had been filled in for twenty years, but apparently nobody ever asked to get off at the Municipal Recreation Facility.

My father moved into a smaller flat that autumn. Sorting his things, we found the original coal route cards in a biscuit tin under a stack of instruction manuals for appliances he no longer owned. There was FLORENCE, in my grandfather’s sloping hand, between GAS LANE and SHORT CUT IF DRY. On the reverse was a list of weights and prices, a drawing of a woman’s shoe, and the words NO CREDIT TO MAN WITH FERRET. My father claimed not to remember the man, the ferret, or the circumstances of the prohibition. I suspect that on this occasion at least he was keeping something to himself.

The cards are in the library now, in an acid-free box that cost more than my grandfather earned on a good day. On Friday afternoons I take the box to my father’s flat, and we choose a route. We do not try to travel it. We sit by the window with the card between us and see how far the conversation goes. Sometimes he remembers a turning and nothing beyond it. Sometimes we spend the whole hour outside one house. Last week he looked at SHORT CUT IF DRY and said, “Never was, though,” and we abandoned the route in favor of a game of cribbage.

People still leave things in the canvas pocket. The other morning I found a note in a young hand: “The place behind the library where my dad lets go of the bike is called by us the place behind the library where my dad lets go of the bike. Sorry it is long.” I took the note upstairs and made a card for it. For location I wrote *east service yard*. For dates of use I wrote *this spring*. Under source, a heading I had never got around to changing, I copied the words *by us*. Then I went to the window. It was nearly closing time. Out in the yard a man was running with one hand extended, a perfectly unnecessary hand, while ahead of him a child on a yellow bicycle rounded the bins and rode on.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION. A literary short story with a sustained narrator’s voice and a carefully developed arc around place-names, memory, and a father’s changing recollections.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant, dryly funny, and tender without becoming sentimental. Its pathos gathers through small acts of attention: a father correcting a detail on a card, a daughter choosing to sit with him over old routes, and a private memory of his mother emerging through the story of a kitchen. The narrator’s practical work of collecting names becomes an invitation to notice how ordinary language holds relationships and local history, even when the official record cannot hold them.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds unofficial names and the people who use them; the gap between maps and lived experience; memory, aging, and family reticence; and the ethics of recording what people say. Its recurring objects—the index cards, route cards, canvas pocket, and pencils—make preservation feel provisional and communal rather than authoritative. The ending returns attention to an everyday scene, suggesting that a place’s meaning can reside in a name as long as the people using it.

## Evidence line
> A dot on a map looks so confident, and a boundary looks more confident still.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — the recurring attention to vernacular language, memory, and modest acts of care is distinctive and sustained throughout this coherent story.
